opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful to start by being a little bit careful about what we mean by "world model," because I don't think it's an all-or-nothing property. The way I tend to think about it is: a model has some kind of world model to the extent that it's maintaining internal representations of the state of the situation being described, and those representations are actually being used to make predictions, in ways that let you go in and manipulate them and see predictable downstream changes in behavior.

And when you frame it that way, the "shallow heuristics" worry and the "world model" claim aren't really mutually exclusive. We've done some work, and there's a lot of nice work from other groups too, looking at things like whether you can decode the state of entities from a model's hidden representations as it reads a description of, say, objects being moved between containers, or a game being played. And what you often find is that, yes, there's a recoverable, causally relevant representation of the state, and it's used for some predictions. But it's also incomplete, it's noisy, and in a lot of cases the model is falling back on surface correlations whenever those happen to be good enough to get the next-token prediction right.

So my view is that these models are learning a kind of patchwork. You have little fragments of something that looks like structured, state-tracking world knowledge, sitting alongside a huge pile of heuristics, and the training objective doesn't really care which one gets used as long as the loss goes down. Humans are arguably like this too, to be honest. We use plenty of shallow heuristics, and we have models of the world that are coherent in some domains and a mess in others.

What I think is interesting scientifically, and important practically, is figuring out when each kind of mechanism is in play. Can we build evaluations that distinguish the cases where the model is genuinely simulating the situation from the ones where it's pattern-matching? Can we intervene on those representations, editing what the model believes about some entity, and get consistent behavior afterward? And can we train in ways that push models toward the more structured, more consistent kind of representation? Because if you want to use these systems for reasoning, planning, or as models of agents, the coherent world model is the part you care about. The heuristics are what make them fail in strange ways once you're slightly off the training distribution.

r001.rationale: The response describes a world model as internal state representations used to predict outcomes, with predictable downstream changes when those representations are manipulated.

r002.rationale: The response does not address whether a world model must reconstruct the full causal process that generated training data.

r003.rationale: It says surface correlations can support predictions, but does not say shallow heuristics support predictions under a restricted class of counterfactual interventions.

r004.rationale: It says heuristics and world models can coexist, but does not frame their disagreement as a terminology dispute rather than a dispute about capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that "world model" is doing a lot of work in that question, and part of what makes the debate confusing is that people mean pretty different things by it. There's a strong version, where a world model means something like a complete, consistent, causal simulator of the environment that the model consults every time it makes a prediction. And then there's a much weaker version, which is just: is there some structure inside the model, some representation, that tracks facts about the state of the world described in the text, and that the model's predictions are causally sensitive to? Those are really different claims, and I think a lot of the arguments people have are actually about which one you're asking about.

My own view is that the evidence for the weak version is pretty good at this point. If you look at things like the Othello work, or some of the work we've done on tracking entity state in text, you can find representations that encode where the pieces are on the board, or whether a box is open or closed, and if you intervene on those representations the model's behavior changes in the way you'd expect. That's not nothing. It's not just n-gram statistics.

But I think the heuristics framing is also right, and the mistake is treating it as an either-or. The way I'd put it is that these models are a mixture. They have some genuinely structured representations of state, and they have an enormous collection of shallow shortcuts, and for any given prediction, which one is actually driving the output depends on the input. If the surface features line up with the shortcut, the shortcut probably wins, because it's cheaper. The structured representation shows up most clearly when you construct inputs where the heuristics give you the wrong answer and the model still gets it right. And sometimes it doesn't. That's the thing to be honest about: having a world model somewhere inside the network doesn't mean the model is using it.

Which, by the way, is also a decent description of people. Humans are famously full of shallow heuristics, and we don't usually say that means humans don't have world models. We say the world model is there and the heuristics sometimes override it. So I think the interesting scientific question isn't "world model, yes or no," it's more like: what's the coverage of the structured representation, how reliable is it, under what conditions does the model actually route its prediction through it versus around it, and can we do anything, either at training time or at inference time, to make it rely on the structured thing more often. That's a question you can actually get traction on empirically, whereas the yes-or-no version tends to just turn into a definitional argument.

r001.rationale: The response describes representations that track world states and affect behavior, but does not present a simplified dynamical model as an appropriate conception of a world model.

r002.rationale: It says a model can have a world model without using it for every prediction, but does not address reconstructing the causal process that generated the training data.

r003.rationale: It says shortcuts can drive predictions when surface features line up, but does not connect that claim to a restricted class of counterfactual interventions.

r004.rationale: The response says people mean different things by “world model” and that the yes-or-no debate tends to become definitional, framing that dispute as one about meaning.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two questions that are useful to separate. One is: does the model represent something about the world? And the other is: does it actually use that representation to make a particular prediction? Those can have different answers.

Suppose you’re training a model to predict text about objects moving around in a room. One way to do that is to keep track of where the objects are. Another is to pick up on regularities in how people describe movement. And a model might do both: it might have information about the objects’ locations available internally, but still rely on a shallow cue when that cue is enough to get the next word right.

So I don’t think finding a heuristic necessarily establishes that there’s no world model. But showing that you can decode some fact from the model’s activations doesn’t establish that it’s using a world model, either. You’d like to intervene: change the situation in a way that breaks the superficial regularity, or change the internal representation, and see whether the predictions change in the way you’d expect.

The interesting question to me is less whether there’s a world model, as a yes-or-no property, and more what the model tracks, how consistently it tracks it, and when that information actually guides its behavior.

r001.rationale: It gives tracking object locations as one possible way to predict movement text, but does not present a simplified dynamical model as an appropriate conception of a world model.

r002.rationale: It does not address whether a world model must reconstruct the full causal process that generated the training data.

r003.rationale: It says a shallow cue may suffice for a prediction and proposes interventions that break superficial regularities, but does not state that heuristics support predictions under a restricted class of counterfactual interventions.

r004.rationale: It frames the issue as what the model tracks and when that information guides behavior, but does not characterize the dispute as one of terminology rather than capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be a little careful about what we mean by a world model. A system can have information about the world that’s useful for making predictions without having a single, coherent representation that it consults every time it answers a question.

Suppose a model correctly predicts what happens when you drop a glass. It might be representing something about gravity and fragility, or it might have seen lots of sentences about glasses falling and breaking. That particular prediction doesn’t distinguish those explanations. And both mechanisms might be available in the same model: sometimes it uses a shortcut, and sometimes it does something more like reasoning about the situation.

So I’d want to ask more specific questions. What information does the model represent? Does that information actually play a causal role in its predictions? And can it use that information when we change the setup in a way that makes familiar shortcuts unreliable?

The fact that a model uses shallow heuristics isn’t, by itself, evidence that it has no world model. People use shallow heuristics all the time. But getting a lot of predictions right isn’t sufficient evidence for a rich world model either. The interesting thing is figuring out what structure it has learned and when it actually uses it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses useful world information and possible representations, but does not present a simplified dynamical model as the appropriate conception.

r002.rationale: It does not state that a world model need not reconstruct the full causal process that generated the training data.

r003.rationale: It mentions changing a setup so familiar shortcuts become unreliable, but does not say shallow heuristics can support predictions under a restricted class of counterfactual interventions.

r004.rationale: The response says we should be careful about what “world model” means, but does not characterize the disagreement as terminology rather than capability.
